_note: Every open-source module, standard, open-weights model and commercial speech provider that ThusoIQ Master v3.5 names in §15D, §20, §23 and §45, with the decision the specification made for each, the engine, routes, doors and capabilities in this repository it would plug into, and what stands in its way. The founder asked on 14 September 2026 for the modules on the specification to be linked as detailed. Linking is registering: no code from any of these is in this repository, no manifest declares one, and no service calls one. docs/OPEN-SOURCE.md is generated from this file, the status page renders it, and the open-source register section of scripts/check-boundaries.mjs holds it to its rules.
_honestyNote: Every source field was read from the primary source on verifiedOn — the repository's LICENSE file and GitHub API, the publisher's page, or the vendor's public documentation — or it is null with unverified: true and a sentence saying why. Nothing here is a guess. A licence that changed, a missing LICENSE file and a model that forbids commercial use are recorded because they were found, and they are the most useful lines in the file.
_dependencyMarkersNote: dependencyMarkers are the names under which a component would appear in a package manifest. They are what the dependency check searches for, alongside the repository URL; they are not claims about the component.

kinds.meaning: Software with a public repository and a licence file, which MyThuso could run.
A published specification MyThuso would implement, not software it would run.
A list or a category used to find components, not a component.
A vendor sold under contract. Not open source.
A model whose weights are published under a stated licence, to be fine-tuned and run where MyThuso controls it.
A vendor the specification declined, recorded so the decision is auditable and cannot be quietly reversed.

decisions.meaning: §15D: to be adopted and self-hosted where it covers the need, after review. Not adopted yet.
§15D: to be adopted only behind a restricted, consent-aware gateway with an allow-list. Not adopted yet.
§15D: patterns to read and adapt, never a component that runs as it is.
§15D: accelerators for a supervised pilot, subject to licensing, security and clinical workflow validation.
§15D: for prototypes and test harnesses. Never the diagnostic or triage engine.
§15D: Awesome Health is a directory for discovery and comparison, and the components shortlisted from it are candidates rather than decisions.
§15D: at least two models evaluated, routed by risk, cost and latency behind a model gateway, versioned, with a fallback. No single model becomes GilbertOne.
§15D: the first South African speech candidate to evaluate for a GilbertOne voice pilot, before any contract.
§15D: benchmarked against the primary candidate on the same clinical speech corpus.
§15D: one global voice stack kept as an engineering benchmark and a fallback, never the architecture.
§45: the idea is right and the source was wrong, so open-weights speech models are fine-tuned locally in place of a licensed foreign cloud model.

§20 and §23 name these as the standards the Passport is stored and exchanged in. The specification makes no adopt-or-reference decision for a standard, so this register's term is used rather than one the document does not contain.
§45: the source is refused, with the reason, and what is done instead.

owned.name: GilbertOne orchestration service
owned.what: Conversation state, tool permissions, patient context assembly, care workflow orchestration, escalation, audit and product experience.

refusal.statement: No module, framework or model replaces GilbertOne's orchestration.
refusal.why: §15D calls it the core IP. A module under it can be swapped; the thing that decides which tool a model may call cannot be somebody else's.

owned.name: Clinical policy & triage
owned.what: SATS-aligned triage, red-flag rules, Formulary checks, the protocol registry, Sentinel thresholds and human sign-off policy.

refusal.statement: No module sets a triage priority, a red-flag rule or a Sentinel threshold.
refusal.why: §15D: generative AI may explain; it may not lower a rule-engine priority. The governed SATS and condition protocols remain authoritative.

owned.name: Sentinel's patient-baseline alerting
owned.what: Patient-baseline deviation models under MyThuso's clinical protocols, consuming device data through vendor APIs.

refusal.statement: No vendor's anomaly-detection framework replaces Sentinel.
refusal.why: §45: the alerting logic is the moat MyThuso must own, and the frameworks proposed for it are not licensed to third parties.

procurementRules.statement: No external component gets direct, unrestricted access to the Health Passport; all access flows through ThusoIQ identity, consent, purpose-of-use and audit controls.
procurementRules.why: §16: a breach of the record cannot be undone, and every engine already reads it through one gateway. A module is not an exception to that because somebody else wrote it.

procurementRules.statement: Open source does not mean production-approved; licence, security, maintenance, dependency, vulnerability, data-flow and clinical-use reviews come before adoption.
procurementRules.why: A public repository says who can read the code, not who has checked it. Three of the six Momentum repositories have had no commit for more than a year, and one has no licence file at all.

procurementRules.statement: Model and provider abstraction is kept from day one: standard request and response schemas, a model registry, feature flags, shadow evaluation and rollback.
procurementRules.why: §15D: no single model becomes GilbertOne. A provider wired straight into a screen is a provider that cannot be withdrawn the day it fails.

procurementRules.statement: Patient audio and transcripts are health information when they reveal symptoms or conditions, and get the Passport's data-minimisation, retention, encryption and consent discipline.
procurementRules.why: A voice describing chest pain is special personal information under POPIA section 26 whichever vendor transcribed it.

procurementRules.statement: No internet-search answer becomes clinical advice at runtime; clinical answers are grounded in versioned, governance-approved protocols, Formulary data and patient-specific facts.
procurementRules.why: §15D: web research is a content-development activity, not the care pathway.

procurementRules.statement: Local-language performance is measured with real South African speakers across age, gender, accent, code-switching, noise, low-bandwidth calls, medicine names and emergency phrases before launch.
procurementRules.why: §15D's launch language gate: marketing support is not the same as clinical readiness.

rules.statement: Nothing in this register is adopted until its licence, security, maintenance, data-flow and clinical-use reviews are each recorded.
rules.why: §15D: open source does not mean production-approved. A module named in a specification is a candidate, and somebody reading its name beside MyThuso's should not come away believing it runs here.

rules.statement: A licence, a URL or a date of last activity is recorded as it was read from the primary source on a stated day, or it is null with the reason it could not be read.
rules.why: A guessed licence is how copyleft code ends up inside a product that cannot publish its source, and a guessed URL is how a typo-squatted package gets installed.

rules.statement: No module reaches the record engine except through the Passport's consent gateway.
rules.why: §15D's first procurement rule, and §16's design test: if a module were compromised, it must not hold the records.

rules.statement: A module driven by a model reads the record only through GilbertOne's allow-listed tools, and never writes to it.
rules.why: §15D: never expose a generic FHIR CRUD tool directly to the patient-facing model. A write tool in front of a model is a record anybody can edit by typing.

rules.statement: Nothing registered as a prototype, a pilot or a reference links the triage route.
rules.why: §15D: Diagnostipy is for prototypes and test harnesses, and clinical policy and triage are owned. A weighted score that reaches the triage route is a diagnosis nobody governs.

rules.statement: A vendor the specification declined is linked to no engine, route or door, and is never adopted.
rules.why: §45 records why each was declined so the decision is auditable. A link would be the first step of reversing it without anybody deciding to.

rules.statement: No package manifest in this repository declares a registered component.
rules.why: Adoption starts with the five reviews. A dependency added to try something is adoption that skipped them, and it is found by the build rather than by an audit.

rules.statement: A door a link needs and packages/catalog/feeds.json does not have is written as proposed, with what must be true before it opens, and only for as long as it is absent.
rules.why: A link to a door that does not exist reads as a seam that works. Once the door is declared, the link names it by its real id and its real conditions.

rules.statement: What MyThuso owns is never marked replaceable, and no component is registered as replacing it.
rules.why: §15D: own the patient experience, clinical policy, orchestration, safety, data model and audit trail; rent or replace what sits underneath.

proposedDoors.why: §26 names POST /hl7v2/inbound, and packages/catalog/apis/record.json holds it as a door to add because the caller is a partner's system.

beforeSwitchOn.must: Each partner connects over mutual TLS under an agreement that defines its operator role.
beforeSwitchOn.why: §22 and §25: a hospital or a laboratory is a separate responsible party, and a certificate names which one sent a message.

beforeSwitchOn.must: Every ADT, ORU and ORM message is mapped to FHIR with Provenance naming the source system before anything is written.
beforeSwitchOn.why: §20: lab-confirmed and self-reported data must always be distinguishable.

beforeSwitchOn.must: A message whose patient cannot be matched is held for a person, never matched by a best guess.
beforeSwitchOn.why: A result filed against the wrong patient is two clinical errors at once.

proposedDoors.why: §15D's sixth runtime layer — primary and fallback models, a prompt and model registry, output-schema validation — is declared by no contract in this repository.

beforeSwitchOn.must: At least two models are evaluated and a fallback is named for every task routed to one.
Every call records the model, prompt and protocol version it ran on.
beforeSwitchOn.why: §15D's audit layer: without the version, a harmful answer cannot be traced or reproduced.

beforeSwitchOn.must: A hosted model processes in South Africa, or a section 72 determination names where, under a data processing agreement.
beforeSwitchOn.why: A prompt carrying a patient's symptoms is special personal information in transit.

beforeSwitchOn.must: The clinical safety layer runs before any model output reaches a person, and nothing a model returns lowers an urgency.
beforeSwitchOn.why: §15D: allowed actions and minimum urgency are set by rules; the model cannot override downward.

proposedDoors.why: §23's fourth integration path registers the Passport with the national exchange as a point-of-service system and matches patients through HPRS. No feed or route declares it.

beforeSwitchOn.must: The National Department of Health publishes the integration profile the Passport would conform to, and it is named here.
beforeSwitchOn.why: No official source naming a national exchange or an OpenHIM profile could be found on 14 September 2026; a door built to a guess is the door that is rebuilt.

beforeSwitchOn.must: Only the summary set the Department specifies is shared, and no sealed category.
beforeSwitchOn.why: §20: sealed categories are excluded from every grant unless explicitly included.

components.name: Momentum Open Wearables
components.provides: A self-hosted platform that normalises wearable data from Garmin, Oura, Whoop, Polar, Fitbit and others, and Apple HealthKit, Samsung Health and Health Connect through SDKs, behind one API.

maintenance.what: Release 0.8.0; the last commit seen was on 14 September 2026.

links.how: Self-hosted, it would turn a linked consumer wearable's data into readings posted to the devices engine with their source and quality, each written to the Passport through its gateway, arriving on the wearable-sync door in packages/catalog/feeds.json, which refuses every payload until its switch-on conditions are met.

blockedBy: None of the five reviews has been done.
The wearable-sync door in packages/catalog/feeds.json refuses every payload, and none of its switch-on conditions is met.
Its cloud integrations pull data through each vendor's own cloud by OAuth, and where each vendor processes that data has not been established.
It would be self-hosted, and no hosting in South Africa has been chosen for health data.

refusals.statement: A reading that came through Open Wearables carries no clinical weight and triggers no dispatch.
refusals.why: Full Scope Engine 9, which the devices contract already refuses on.

refusals.statement: Open Wearables does not stand in for the direct adapters for BP cuffs, CGM, SpO₂ or the Thuso Pod.
refusals.why: §15D: keep direct adapters where Open Wearables does not cover the device or the clinical-grade data path.

components.name: Momentum FHIR MCP Server
components.provides: An MCP server that lets language-model agents read and write a FHIR server, with terminology lookup and document search.

maintenance.what: Release 0.1.0, its only release; the last commit seen was on 13 October 2025.

links.how: GilbertOne would reach it only as named tools on the allow-list behind POST /v1/access/tools/{tool}, and it would read the Passport's FHIR routes through the consent gateway under the patient's grant; it writes nothing.

blockedBy: None of the five reviews has been done.
As shipped, document search requires a Pinecone API key and terminology lookup may call the LOINC API, so it would send data to services outside South Africa.
One release, on 23 October 2025, and no commit since 13 October 2025.
GilbertOne's tool gateway is proposed, not built, and its allow-list names no FHIR tool.

refusals.statement: The FHIR MCP Server is never offered to GilbertOne as a general-purpose record tool; it is reached as named, read-only tools.
refusals.why: §15D: never expose a generic FHIR CRUD tool directly to the patient-facing model.

refusals.statement: A tool it offers that is not on GilbertOne's allow-list is refused.
refusals.why: §15D: a restricted, consent-aware tool gateway with an allow-list.

refusals.statement: No part of a patient's record is indexed in an external vector store or sent to an external terminology service.
refusals.why: Its README requires Pinecone for document search and calls the LOINC API; either would move special personal information across a border without a section 72 basis.

components.name: Momentum HealthStack
components.provides: Terraform modules for building healthcare infrastructure on AWS, with WAF, HealthLake, S3, KMS, VPN, CloudTrail, VPC and Fargate modules.

maintenance.what: Last commit c8b43e2; no releases published.

components.unlinkedBecause: Infrastructure-as-code patterns are read and adapted, not called; no engine, route or door would ever reach them.

blockedBy: None of the five reviews has been done.
It is written for AWS alone and for HIPAA; POPIA and South African data residency are not mentioned.
No hosting provider, region, key custody or disaster-recovery decision has been made for health data.

refusals.statement: A HIPAA-oriented reference stack is not taken as meeting POPIA, South African data residency, key management, disaster recovery or audit requirements.
refusals.why: §15D: do not assume a HIPAA-oriented reference stack is automatically sufficient for South Africa.

refusals.statement: No hosting decision follows from HealthStack being written for AWS.
refusals.why: docs/PRIVACY-AND-SECURITY.md records that no residency decision has been made, and a module's defaults are not how one gets made.

components.name: Momentum Notetaker
components.provides: Transcription and summarisation that turn a spoken consultation into structured notes, running Whisper and Ollama locally.

maintenance.what: Last commit 68cf86c; no releases published.

source.unverifiedReason: The README shows an MIT badge and says to see LICENSE, but the repository has no LICENSE file — GitHub's licence API returns 404 and blob/main/LICENSE does not exist — so there is no licence grant to rely on.

links.how: It would draft the subjective, objective, assessment and plan sections of a structured consultation from consented audio; the clinician edits the draft and signs, and nothing it wrote is part of the record until they do.

blockedBy: The repository has no LICENSE file, so it cannot be used at all until the authors add one.
No commit since 22 May 2025.
None of the five reviews has been done.
Speaker separation needs a Hugging Face key and gated pyannote models, and recording a consultation is refused in the preview with no consent to record in place.

refusals.statement: A scribe's draft is never signed by software and never enters the record until a clinician has read, edited and signed it.
refusals.why: §15D: human sign-off policy is owned, and generative AI may explain but not decide.

refusals.statement: Consultation audio is never sent to a hosted transcription API; only local mode is considered.
refusals.why: Its README offers the OpenAI API as an option; a consultation's audio is health information under §15D's procurement rules, whichever vendor hears it.

components.name: Momentum FHIRBoard
components.provides: A Docker-packaged analytics playground that turns FHIR ViewDefinitions into SQL over FHIR export files, with DuckDB and Superset for charts.

maintenance.what: Last commit 2ef6c32; no releases published.

links.noSeamBecause: No contract defines a de-identified extract, and §25 allows secondary use only de-identified under a governance committee that does not yet exist, so there is nothing a dashboard could lawfully read.
links.how: It would read only a de-identified FHIR export produced under §25's secondary-use governance, for clinical governance dashboards, and never the Passport.

blockedBy: None of the five reviews has been done.
No de-identification method, secondary-use committee or de-identified extract exists.
No commit since 28 May 2025.

refusals.statement: FHIRBoard reads de-identified exports only and never connects to the Passport or any store of identifiable records.
refusals.why: §25: secondary use is de-identified only, with no re-identification.

refusals.statement: No governance dashboard shows or exports a row about one person.
refusals.why: §25: never at record level. A dashboard filter narrow enough to find one patient is a record lookup with a chart on it.

components.name: Momentum Diagnostipy
components.provides: A Python library for rule-based diagnosis from symptom rules and rulesets, with adjustable scoring and confidence functions.

maintenance.what: Last commit 27f517d; no releases published.

links.noSeamBecause: It is a prototype and test-harness library, run against packages/mock-api on synthetic cases only; the route it most resembles is the triage route it may never reach.
links.how: It could help script synthetic cases for the clinical red-team in weeks 6 to 10 of the 90-day proof-of-architecture and exercise the mock's triage refusals, and nothing more.

blockedBy: Prototype only by decision: there is no production use to unblock.
No commit since 4 December 2024, and no clinical or regulatory validation.

refusals.statement: Diagnostipy never links to POST /v1/clinical/triage and never produces a priority, a diagnosis or a care setting a person is shown.
refusals.why: §15D: do not treat it as the final diagnostic or triage engine; governed SATS and condition protocols remain authoritative.

refusals.statement: No weight or score from Diagnostipy is written into the protocol registry.
refusals.why: packages/catalog/protocols.json refuses a draft carrying any threshold; clinical content comes from the Medical Director and the governance board.

components.name: Awesome Health
components.provides: A curated list of open-source healthcare software, libraries, tools and resources, in sections such as EHR, specifications, prescribing, nursing and imaging.

maintenance.what: Last commit 912dbe0; no releases published.

components.unlinkedBecause: It is a directory of links, not software; the components shortlisted from it are registered as entries of their own.

blockedBy: Nothing to adopt: it is a list, and its last commit was on 2 July 2023, so its judgement that each project is active needs checking again.

refusals.statement: A project's appearing in Awesome Health is never taken as evidence that it is maintained, safe or fit for clinical use.
refusals.why: §15D: a curated directory, not a runtime platform or an AI Doctor. Its own claim that every link was vetted as active dates from 2023.

components.name: HAPI FHIR
components.provides: A Java library for building HL7 FHIR clients and servers, with a ready-to-deploy JPA server starter.

maintenance.what: Release v8.12.1.

links.how: It could be the FHIR R4 store and validator behind the Passport's /fhir/* routes and the FHIR validator in §26's conformance suite, with every call still arriving at the consent gateway first.

blockedBy: None of the five reviews has been done.
apps/passport is a zero-dependency Node service; putting a Java FHIR server behind it is an architecture decision for a Head of Engineering, not a registration.
No DPIA, hosting or key custody exists for any clinical store.

refusals.statement: A HAPI FHIR server's own REST endpoint is never reachable; only the Passport's gateway talks to it.
refusals.why: §16: there is no code path that reads a record without a grant, a break-glass justification or the patient's own session.

components.name: OpenHIM
components.provides: The Open Health Information Mediator: an interoperability layer that routes, authenticates and logs traffic between health systems.

maintenance.what: Release v8.5.0; commits continued to 15 July 2026 with no newer release.

links.how: If the national exchange runs on OpenHIM, the Passport would register with it as a point-of-service system, and traffic from it would enter through a national-exchange door and the consent gateway rather than any route of its own.

blockedBy: None of the five reviews has been done.
No official source from the National Department of Health names a national health information exchange or an OpenHIM integration profile.
No release since v8.5.0 on 16 September 2024.

refusals.statement: Nothing says MyThuso is connected to, or conformant with, a national health information exchange.
refusals.why: §27 puts national registration at Release 3, and no published profile exists to conform to.

components.name: NextGen Connect (Mirth Connect)
components.provides: An integration engine that receives, transforms and routes HL7 v2 and FHIR messages between clinical systems.

source.licenceNote: MPL-2.0 applies to 4.5.2, the last open-source release. NextGen's FAQ states that on 19 March 2025, with version 4.6, Mirth Connect moved to a single commercial and proprietary licence and source code is no longer published for new releases.

maintenance.what: Release 4.5.2, the last open-source release; the open repository has had no push since.

alternative.name: Open Integration Engine
alternative.note: A community fork made after Mirth Connect became proprietary. Not named by the specification and not reviewed.

links.how: An integration engine would receive a partner's ADT, ORU and ORM messages over mutual TLS and map them to FHIR at §26's POST /hl7v2/inbound, which the record contract holds as a door to add rather than a route.

blockedBy: Mirth Connect is no longer open source from 4.6, and the last open release, 4.5.2 of 23 September 2024, receives no fixes.
Its maintained open fork, Open Integration Engine, is not named by the specification and has not been reviewed.
The hl7v2-inbound door does not exist, and no hospital group or laboratory has agreed to send anything.

refusals.statement: No Mirth Connect release after 4.5.2 is treated as open source.
refusals.why: NextGen's own FAQ: from 4.6 the licence is commercial and proprietary and source is no longer made available.

refusals.statement: No HL7 v2 message is written to the record except as FHIR mapped at the gateway, with Provenance.
refusals.why: §23: ADT, ORU and ORM are mapped to FHIR at the gateway.

components.name: OpenMRS
components.provides: The core API and web application of an open-source medical record system widely used in low-resource settings.

source.licenceNote: The LICENSE file is the full MPL 2.0 text followed by a Healthcare Disclaimer incorporated into its terms. SPDX has no identifier for the disclaimer, so plain MPL-2.0 would understate it.

maintenance.what: Release 2.7.6; the repository was last pushed on 14 September 2026.

links.how: A facility running OpenMRS would connect to the Passport as a SMART on FHIR client under a consent artefact, reading and writing through the gateway like any hospital system; MyThuso would not run it.

blockedBy: No partner facility running it has been identified.
None of the five reviews has been done.

refusals.statement: MyThuso does not run OpenMRS or OpenEMR as its own record; the Passport is the record.
refusals.why: §16: the Passport is its own module with its own service, store and keys, and no other system holds a copy.

components.name: OpenEMR
components.provides: An electronic health record and practice-management system.

source.licenceNote: GitHub reports GPL-3.0 and the file is the GNU GPL version 3; whether it is -only or -or-later was not confirmed.

maintenance.what: Release v8_4_0.

links.how: A practice running OpenEMR would connect to the Passport as a SMART on FHIR client under a consent artefact; MyThuso would not run it.

blockedBy: No partner practice running it has been identified.
None of the five reviews has been done.

refusals.statement: No OpenEMR code is combined into a MyThuso service; a practice running it is a client of the Passport.
refusals.why: GPL-3.0 would oblige MyThuso to publish the source of the combined work, and the Passport's gateway is the boundary that keeps the two apart.

components.name: DICOM
components.provides: The standard for medical imaging data and its communication.

source.licenceTerms: NEMA owns the copyright; the terms allow downloading and copying for informational or personal use only, and any other use needs NEMA's prior written consent.

maintenance.what: Edition 2026c was current when read.

components.unlinkedBecause: No engine contract has an imaging route or door, and nothing in MyThuso's scope stores or moves a DICOM image today.

blockedBy: No imaging service, partner or route exists to use it.

refusals.statement: A wound or foot-diary photograph is not presented as diagnostic imaging.
refusals.why: §15D keeps camera use inside the Track A and B claim boundary; DICOM imaging would be a different, regulated service.

components.name: Lab and PHR components
components.provides: A category the specification asks to be shortlisted from Awesome Health: laboratory and personal health record components.

source.unverifiedReason: §15D names a category rather than a component, so there is no repository, licence or activity to read until somebody shortlists one.

components.unlinkedBecause: Nothing is named yet; laboratory results would arrive on the lab-result door the medicines contract lists to add.

blockedBy: No component has been shortlisted.

components.name: Reasoning and multimodal language models
components.provides: Draft explanations, summaries, questions and low-risk guidance for GilbertOne, behind a model gateway.

source.unverifiedReason: §15D names no model and requires at least two to be evaluated, so there is no provider to look up until a shortlist exists.

links.how: A model would draft GilbertOne's words behind a model gateway with a registry of models and prompts, output-schema validation and a fallback, and would reach another engine only as an allow-listed tool.

blockedBy: No model is shortlisted and the model-gateway door does not exist.
GilbertOne gives approved answers only today, and no clinical governance has approved generated ones.

refusals.statement: Nothing a model returns lowers a priority the rules set.
refusals.why: §15D: generative AI may explain; it may not lower a rule-engine priority.

refusals.statement: A model is never given a general-purpose record tool.
refusals.why: §15D: never expose a generic FHIR CRUD tool directly to the patient-facing model.

refusals.statement: No single model or provider becomes GilbertOne.
refusals.why: §15D: evaluate at least two, version every model and prompt, and keep a fallback.

components.name: Botlhale AI speech APIs
components.provides: Speech-to-text and text-to-speech APIs listing Tshivenda, isiZulu, Afrikaans, Sesotho, isiXhosa, Setswana, Sepedi, Xitsonga, Siswati, isiNdebele, Swahili and Kinyarwanda.

maintenance.what: The public speech APIs page loaded and was read; a vendor's release history is not public.

links.how: A transcript of one push-to-talk turn would arrive on the speech-transcript door, for the person to correct before it is sent to GilbertOne.

blockedBy: No contract and no data processing agreement.
Every condition on the speech-transcript door is unmet: an agreement, South African processing and no audio kept.
Its speech APIs page does not list South African English, which §15D says it covers; that needs confirming with the vendor.
Medical vocabulary, noisy homes, older voices, mixed-language speech and end-to-end latency are untested.

refusals.statement: No patient audio is sent to Botlhale AI before a contract and a data processing agreement exist.
refusals.why: §15D: patient audio and transcripts are health information when they reveal symptoms or conditions.

components.name: Lelapa AI Vulavula
components.provides: Speech-to-text and translation for isiZulu, Sesotho, Afrikaans, South African English and other languages, with a self-hosted enterprise option on Kubernetes or OpenShift.

maintenance.what: The public documentation loaded and was read; a vendor's release history is not public.

links.how: Hosted or self-hosted in a South African cluster, its transcript of a turn would arrive on the same speech-transcript door, benchmarked against Botlhale on the same corpus.

blockedBy: No contract and no data processing agreement; the self-hosted path is sized and licensed by the vendor on request.
Every condition on the speech-transcript door is unmet.
No consented, de-identified six-language health speech corpus exists for the bake-off.

refusals.statement: No patient audio is sent to Lelapa AI before a contract and a data processing agreement exist.
refusals.why: §15D: patient audio and transcripts are health information when they reveal symptoms or conditions.

components.name: Global speech and voice stack
components.provides: One global voice stack kept as an engineering benchmark and a fallback.

source.unverifiedReason: §15D names no vendor for the fallback, so there is nothing to look up until one is chosen.

links.how: A benchmark or fallback transcript would arrive on the speech-transcript door under exactly the conditions a local provider's would.

blockedBy: No vendor is chosen, and every condition on the speech-transcript door is unmet.

refusals.statement: No consumer assistant — Google Assistant, Siri or Bixby — becomes GilbertOne's voice architecture.
refusals.why: §15D's recommendation: do not make any consumer assistant or single model the architecture.

components.name: OpenAI Whisper
components.provides: A multilingual speech-recognition and speech-translation model with its inference code.

source.licenceNote: The README states that Whisper's code and model weights are released under the MIT License. The Hugging Face card for whisper-large-v3 is tagged apache-2.0; the repository's own statement is recorded.

maintenance.what: Release v20250625; the repository was last pushed on 31 August 2026.

links.how: Fine-tuned locally and run on the phone or in a South African cluster, its transcript of a turn would reach GilbertOne the way a provider's does, on the speech-transcript door or heard on the device.

blockedBy: No consented, community-recorded South African speech corpus exists to fine-tune it on.
No fine-tuning partnership with Lelapa AI, Masakhane, the CSIR or a university lab exists.
None of the five reviews has been done.

refusals.statement: The open weights run where MyThuso controls them; a hosted transcription API is not what §45 adopted.
refusals.why: §45: patient voice is special personal information, and open weights give the head start without routing it through somebody else's cloud.

components.name: Meta MMS (Massively Multilingual Speech)
components.provides: Speech recognition, speech synthesis and language identification for more than 1,000 languages.

source.licenceNote: The MMS README states that the MMS code and model weights are released under CC-BY-NC 4.0, overriding fairseq's MIT licence for MMS; the Hugging Face models are tagged the same.

maintenance.what: The fairseq repository is archived; its last push was on 30 September 2025.

links.how: Its transcript of a turn would reach GilbertOne on the speech-transcript door, as any speech model's would.

blockedBy: CC-BY-NC-4.0 covers its code and weights, so a paid health service cannot use it without a separate licence from Meta.
fairseq is archived and receives no fixes.
No consented South African speech corpus or fine-tuning partnership exists.

refusals.statement: MMS is not used in anything MyThuso charges for while its licence is non-commercial.
refusals.why: CC-BY-NC-4.0 forbids commercial use, and a health service a patient pays for is commercial use.

components.name: Meta Seamless (SeamlessM4T)
components.provides: Foundation models for speech-to-speech, speech-to-text and text translation.

source.licenceNote: Three licences: MIT for the code and some components, CC-BY-NC-4.0 for the SeamlessM4T and SeamlessStreaming models, and a custom Seamless Licensing Agreement for the Seamless and SeamlessExpressive models.

maintenance.what: Last push; no releases published.

links.how: Its transcript or translation of a turn would reach GilbertOne on the speech-transcript door, as any speech model's would.

blockedBy: The speech models themselves are CC-BY-NC-4.0 or under a custom agreement, so they are not available for a paid service without a separate licence.
No consented South African speech corpus or fine-tuning partnership exists.

refusals.statement: No Seamless model under a non-commercial or custom licence is used in anything MyThuso charges for.
refusals.why: CC-BY-NC-4.0 forbids commercial use, and the custom agreement has not been read by counsel.

components.name: Google's African-language speech work
components.provides: Open African-language speech resources from Google, as §45 describes them without naming one.

source.unverifiedReason: §45 does not name a model or dataset. The most plausible open resource, the WAXAL dataset, is licensed CC-BY-4.0 or CC-BY-SA-4.0 by data provider and lists no South African language; if the sentence meant another Google model, no licence was verified for it.

links.how: Anything trained from it would reach GilbertOne on the speech-transcript door, as any speech model's would.

blockedBy: Which Google resource §45 means has to be decided before anything about it can be reviewed.
WAXAL, the likeliest candidate, covers none of the six launch languages.

components.name: HL7 FHIR R4
components.provides: HL7's resource and REST standard for exchanging healthcare data, which the Passport is stored and exchanged in.

maintenance.what: Version 4.0.1 (Technical Correction 1). The page states that 5.0.0 supersedes it; §20 tracks R5.

links.how: The Passport's /fhir/* routes read and write R4-shaped resources, with Provenance on every write, behind the consent gateway.

blockedBy: The Passport P0 writes FHIR-shaped resources, and §26's FHIR validator conformance suite has not been run against them.

refusals.statement: A resource shaped like FHIR is not called conformant until §26's FHIR validator suite passes.
refusals.why: §26: the Passport ships its own conformance suite, and a hospital integrator will run the validator whether or not MyThuso does.

components.name: SMART on FHIR (SMART App Launch)
components.provides: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect profiles for authorising apps and systems against FHIR servers with scopes.

maintenance.what: Version 2.2.0 (STU 2.2), marked current.

links.how: A hospital or practice system would connect as an authorised SMART client and read and write FHIR resources under a consent artefact, with discharge summaries and results flowing back into the Passport.

blockedBy: No partner system, no client registration and no mutual TLS exist.

refusals.statement: A SMART scope never stands in for the patient's consent artefact; both are checked on every call.
refusals.why: §21 and §26: the gateway validates the consent artefact on every request, whatever token the caller holds.

components.name: HL7 Version 2 (ADT, ORU, ORM)
components.provides: The messaging standard most South African private hospital groups and laboratories still speak for admissions, results and orders.

source.unverifiedReason: HL7's product page and its free-IP FAQ answered with a web-application-firewall challenge and no content, so neither the current version nor the terms could be read.

links.how: ADT, ORU and ORM messages from partner systems would arrive on the hl7v2-inbound door and be mapped to FHIR at the gateway. In development (Wave 5) the Passport P0 answers §26's POST /hl7v2/inbound for a developer sending a registered synthetic partner's ADT A01, A03 or ORU R01, read by a parser written in this repository rather than by any HL7 library.

blockedBy: The hl7v2-inbound door does not exist and no hospital group or laboratory has agreed to connect.
The development route takes synthetic messages from two registered synthetic partners only, over HTTP on the loopback, and serves no MLLP.

refusals.statement: No integration plan with a South African hospital group or laboratory assumes FHIR alone.
refusals.why: §20: most SA private hospital groups and labs still speak HL7 v2, and the bridge is not optional.

refusals.statement: No HL7 v2 library is declared by any manifest; the few segments the Passport reads are read by code written here.
refusals.why: §15D: open source does not mean production-approved, and no HL7 library has had its licence, security, maintenance, data-flow or clinical-use review. The Record · HL7 v2 bridge block of scripts/check-boundaries.mjs holds every manifest to it.

components.name: IHE XDS.b and MHD
components.provides: IHE's registry and repository profile for sharing clinical documents between organisations, and its FHIR RESTful counterpart for mobile access.

maintenance.what: MHD 4.2.4 on FHIR R4, the latest trial-use release; XDS.b is in ITI Technical Framework revision 20.2 of 11 November 2025.

source.unverifiedReason: The XDS.b page carries only an IHE International copyright notice, and a CC0 badge was reported on the MHD guide without its wording being seen, so the terms of use are not recorded.

links.how: Where a facility uses document exchange, its documents would be written and found as FHIR DocumentReference resources through the Passport's gateway.

blockedBy: No facility using document exchange has been identified.

components.name: International Patient Summary
components.provides: The minimal cross-border patient summary data set, as the HL7 IPS FHIR guide and ISO 27269.

maintenance.what: HL7 IPS 2.0.1 (STU 2 errata), marked current.

source.unverifiedReason: The HL7 guide's licence wording was not seen directly, and ISO's pages for ISO 27269 returned 403; the IPS editorial team states the ISO standard is not free.

links.how: The emergency summary and the full export would be produced as an International Patient Summary through the Passport.

blockedBy: The export route is proposed, not built, and no export has been validated.

refusals.statement: A sealed category is left out of the International Patient Summary unless the patient opts it in.
refusals.why: §20 and §24: sealed categories are excluded from the default emergency summary.

components.name: SMART Health Links and Cards
components.provides: Encrypted, passcode-protected, expiring links to a health summary, and signed verifiable health credentials in a QR code.

maintenance.what: HL7 SMART Health Cards and Links IG 1.0.0 (STU 1); the Boston Children's Hospital specifications are Health Cards 1.4.0 and Health Links version 1.

links.how: A patient, or a responder during a trip, would create a scoped, expiring, passcode-protected link to the summary; the Passport Card would carry a signed emergency summary as a SMART Health Card.

blockedBy: The share-link route is proposed, not built, and no signing key custody exists.

refusals.statement: The Passport Card is an emergency credential the patient holds, never a credential the state reads.
refusals.why: §45 declined the health-code framing: same outcome, and the framing matters.

refusals.statement: Every share link carries a scope, a passcode and an expiry.
refusals.why: §20 and §26: a permanently valid document is a copy of the record nobody can take back.

components.name: OpenID Connect
components.provides: An identity layer on OAuth 2.0 for signing people in.

source.licenceTerms: The OpenID Foundation grants a non-exclusive, royalty-free, worldwide copyright licence to reproduce and implement the specification, with attribution, under its Appendix C; patents are covered by the Foundation's non-assertion covenant.

maintenance.what: Core 1.0 incorporating errata set 2.

links.how: People would sign in with OpenID Connect, with multi-factor authentication for clinical and admin users; today the identity service signs in with a one-time code.

blockedBy: The identity service issues its own sessions from a one-time code, and no identity provider has been chosen.

refusals.statement: Signing in proves who somebody is and opens no record by itself.
refusals.why: §21: a consent artefact is validated on every request; an identity token is not one.

components.name: National Health Information Exchange (NHIE / OpenHIM) integration profile
components.provides: The national exchange the Passport would register with as a point-of-service system, as §20 and §23 describe it.

source.unverifiedReason: No National Department of Health source naming an NHIE or an OpenHIM integration profile could be found: the 2014 Health Normative Standards Framework (Gazette 37583) calls for a health information exchange without naming one, and the 2019–2024 digital health strategy and the 2026–2027 performance plan do not mention one.

links.how: The Passport would register with the exchange, match patients through HPRS and share the summary set the Department specifies, through a national-exchange door and the gateway.

blockedBy: No published profile to conform to, and §27 puts registration at Release 3 after ISO 27001 and 27799 certification.

components.name: Health Patient Registration System (HPRS)
components.provides: The National Department of Health's patient registry, which issues the Health Patient Registration Number.

source.unverifiedReason: Only planning documents describe HPRS — the 2026–2027 performance plan reports it installed at 3,266 health establishments by March 2025 — and no specification, interface or terms of use were found.

links.how: A patient would be matched to the national registry through the exchange, never by the Passport storing an HPRS number it was not given.

blockedBy: No published interface, and access would be the Department's to grant.

components.name: iFlytek and Baidu acoustic models
components.provides: Instead: open-weights speech models fine-tuned locally with Lelapa AI, Masakhane, the CSIR and university labs on community-recorded data, on the device where possible.

source.unverifiedReason: Declined by §45; nothing about these vendors was looked up, because nothing from them will be used.

blockedBy: Declined by the specification.

refusals.statement: No iFlytek or Baidu acoustic model is licensed, called or run for any MyThuso voice.
refusals.why: §45: patient voice is special personal information; routing it through a Chinese cloud model breaches the Passport's data-residency rule and creates sanctions exposure, because several named vendors are on export-control lists.

components.name: Hikvision and Dahua mmWave radar
components.provides: Instead: radar from neutral mmWave ODMs or Vayyar-class vendors, with all processing on the device and no vendor cloud.

source.unverifiedReason: Declined by §45; nothing about these vendors was looked up, because nothing from them will be used.

blockedBy: Declined by the specification.

refusals.statement: Neither Hikvision nor Dahua supplies a sensor for Ambient Home Mode.
refusals.why: §45: both carry export-control and security baggage that will fail a scheme's or a government's due diligence.

components.name: Huawei and Zepp anomaly-detection frameworks
components.provides: Instead: Sentinel's own patient-baseline deviation models under MyThuso's clinical protocols, consuming device data through vendor APIs.

source.unverifiedReason: Declined by §45; nothing about these frameworks was looked up, because §45 records that they are not licensed to third parties.

blockedBy: Declined by the specification.

refusals.statement: No Huawei or Zepp anomaly-detection framework is licensed; Sentinel's alerting is MyThuso's own.
refusals.why: §45: those frameworks are not licensed to third parties, and the alerting logic is the moat MyThuso must own.
